title: Heap
body:
A complete binary [[Tree]] with the **heap property**: every parent compares correctly
against its children. In a min-heap the parent is smaller than both children, so the minimum
is at the root; in a max-heap it is larger, so the maximum is. That is the entire invariant,
and it is deliberately weaker than a [[Binary Search Tree]]'s. A heap is **not sorted**.
Nothing is guaranteed *between* siblings, and asking a heap whether it contains some
arbitrary value is an $O(n)$ scan.

The point is that you only ever want one end. A heap makes "give me the smallest thing"
cheap and does not waste effort ordering anything else, which is exactly what a priority
queue needs: [[Ready Queue]] scheduling in [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]], Dijkstra's next-nearest
vertex, and the merge step of external sorting.

```
min-heap                 array form
      2                  [2, 4, 7, 9, 5, 11]
    /   \                 0  1  2  3  4   5
   4     7
  / \   /                 children of i: 2i+1, 2i+2
 9   5 11                 parent of i:   (i-1)/2
```

Because the tree is complete (every level full except possibly the last, which fills left to
right), it stores perfectly in an [[Array]] with no pointers at all. Index arithmetic
replaces the links.

## Operations

| Operation | Cost |
|---|---|
| Peek at the root | $O(1)$ |
| Insert | $O(\log n)$ |
| Extract-min (or max) | $O(\log n)$ |
| Build a heap from $n$ items | $O(n)$ |
| Search for an arbitrary value | $O(n)$ |

**Insert** puts the new element at the end of the array (the next free leaf) and *sifts up*:
while it is smaller than its parent, swap. It rises at most the height of the tree, which is
$\log n$.

**Extract-min** takes the root, moves the last element into the root slot, and *sifts down*:
swap with the smaller child until the heap property holds again. Also $\log n$.

Building a heap by repeated insertion is $O(n \log n)$, but sifting down from the middle of
the array backwards is $O(n)$, which is the surprising one and worth remembering.

## Heapsort

Build a max-heap, then repeatedly swap the root with the last element and shrink the heap by
one. The array ends up sorted in place, in $O(n \log n)$ worst case, with no scratch space:
better guarantees than [[Quick Sort]] and better memory than [[Merge Sort]]. It loses in
practice on constants and cache behaviour, which is why it usually appears as the fallback
inside a hybrid sort rather than on its own.
